title: France targets Shein and Temu with fast fashion fees
description: France has started imposing fees on fast fashion items which could reach almost €20 per garment by 2030, as the government tries to curb sales of chea
body: France has started imposing fees on fast fashion items which could reach almost €20 per garment by 2030, as the government tries to curb sales of cheap clothing sold by e-commerce sites.The levy, which came into force on Tuesday, follows a new law passed in June to regulate so-called "ultra-fast fashion" companies such as Shein, Temu and AliExpress.The e-commerce giants, known for selling large volumes of cheap apparel, have been criticised by French officials for driving a surge in fast fashion.China's commerce ministry has described the French law as discriminatory and a trade barrier, saying it could violate World Trade Organization (WTO) principles.French minister Mathieu Lefevre said the "harmful effects of ultra-fast fashion" on the environment and economy were "well known".In July, Lefevre's office said the levy would not apply to retailers such as H&M or Zara, prompting some to say that the measure appeared to spare European companies.Under the legislation, ultra-fast fashion will be determined according to two factors: the volume of clothing placed on the market and the cost of repairing garments relative to their purchase price.The per-item fee will vary on a set scale according to how each product scores on both these standards.For 2026, the charges range from a €0.50 (£0.43) levy on underwear to €2 (£1.71) for T-shirts, to €9 (£7.71) for jeans and €12 (£10.28) for a jacket.The levy could reach up to €19.50 (£16.71/$22.60) per item by 2030, though the cap remains at 50% of the product's pre-tax price.

schema.headline: France targets Shein and Temu with fast fashion fees

title: Sexual assaults in Ceuta happening almost every day, prosecutors say
description: Spanish prosecutors say 23 sexual assaults, including nine against children, have been recorded in Ceuta since the mass influx of migrants into the Sp
body: Spanish prosecutors say 23 sexual assaults, including nine against children, have been recorded in Ceuta since the mass influx of migrants into the Spanish exclave  at the end of July.That number meant there was almost one case every day, Ceuta's chief prosecutor Silvia Rojas said.She told El País newspaper migrant girls were "particularly vulnerable because of their irregular status in the territory".At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July and although most have returned, as many as 5,000 remain - leading to unrest in the autonomous city in North Africa and a crisis for Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.Between 1,400 and 1,600 of the estimated 5,000 migrants still in Ceuta are children, according to Rojas.Among the suspected attackers are four Moroccans, three Spaniards and a Belgian, Efe news agency reports.There have been scenes of violence in recent days as tensions flare up between migrants and local residents. Sánchez called the second meeting of his national security council in a week on Tuesday to tackle the issue.Rojas said the influx had led to an exponential increase in sexual assault, and many victims did not file a report, either out of fear of because of their "current situation in Ceuta". The Spanish Society of Epidemiology said the border crisis had highlighted the difficulty in detecting and tackling violence against migrant women and girls.One 24-year-old woman from Morocco told the BBC she had "put her life in danger" by travelling to Ceuta, and described being sexually assaulted while sleeping among a group of men and women. "I was shocked… If I had known this, I wouldn't have come."Emergency doctor Susana Ascaso said last month her department at Ceuta University Hospital had treated several sexual assault victims, including one who was just 10 years old.Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo said a multi-million euro aid package had been approved by the cabinet that would help provide essential services and cover care for unaccompanied children.The territory's conservative mayor, Juan Jesús Vivas, has called on Spaniards to take part in demonstrations across mainland Spain in support of Ceuta on Wednesday, which coincides with the city's annual holiday.The Spanish government is facing bitter criticism from its opponents for its handling of the crisis. The hard-right Vox party said Sánchez had not "lost control of Ceuta - he has handed it over".Arantxa Campos, president of the Ceuta Employers' Confederation, told the BBC: "We can't do anything unless these people leave. "We don't have a plan from the government. We don't have anything. We don't even know when they're going to finish screening everyone."The prime minister said on Monday that King Felipe VI would visit Ceuta "as soon as conditions allow", seen as an attempt to assert Spanish authority over the exclave. Morocco has a long-standing claim over Ceuta and its fellow autonomous city of Melilla. The last time a Spanish head of state visited the territories in 2007, Rabat pulled its ambassador from Madrid, and another royal visit may cause further diplomatic tensions.In an interview with Spanish radio channel Cadena Ser, Sánchez made a point of saying the king had not visited Ceuta for 20 years - even though Felipe has only been on the throne for 12 years and it was Juan Carlos who visited in 2007. He also asserted he was the only prime minister to have made an official visit to Ceuta while in office, having travelled there on 31 July as the crisis took hold. Some Spanish commentators noted that his remarks appeared to criticise the king, whom he then met later in the day.Unlike his political opponents, Sánchez has been careful to avoid blaming Morocco for stoking the surge of migrants. He said on Monday that no intelligence reports pointed to "any involvement in one way or another" from the Moroccan authorities.Instead he focused on disinformation on social media "associated with both Russia and Israel and an international far-right movement that always uses migration, not only to attack Spain but also Europe". He told Cadena Ser it did not mean "it must come from a state actor" and appeared to indicate the crisis had been stoked after the influx. Government spokeswoman Elma Saiz later confirmed his allegation, saying there was evidence that "various digital forums amplified what happened with the intention of fracturing and polarising Europe".Russia and Israel have both denied any involvement. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar accused the Spanish prime minister of "a blatant lie" and Russia's foreign ministry spokeswoman demanded proof to support Sánchez's allegations.A large number of social media posts appeared in August portraying the border fence between Morocco and Ceuta as safe and easy, even though at least 100 people died while trying to swim around the border fence, according to figures from the mayor.Spanish fact-checking website Maldita said before 30 July, when the influx began, messages circulated on Moroccan social media encouraging people to attempt the crossing, after a June ruling by Spain's Supreme Court.The opposition People's Party (PP) has criticised Sánchez for "exonerating" Morocco and pointing the finger in other directions. Borja Sémper, a spokesperson for the party, said tens of thousands of people could not have moved towards the Ceuta border without Morocco's knowledge.Morocco has denied orchestrating or being involved in the mass crossing.

schema.headline: Sexual assaults in Ceuta happening almost every day, prosecutors say

title: Alps murders: Luger in a lake gives hope for French cold case
description: Police investigating the unsolved murder of a British family in France 14 years ago have an unexpected new clue with the discovery of a Luger pistol i
body: Police investigating the unsolved murder of a British family in France 14 years ago have an unexpected new clue with the discovery of a Luger pistol in the waters of a nearby lake.One of the few certainties in the killings of Saad al-Hilli with his wife and mother-in-law – as well as a passing cyclist – is that they were shot through the head with a Luger model P06, a type used by the Swiss army until around 1960.Now France's cold case unit has confirmed the discovery of a Luger in Lake Annecy,  not far from the scene of the murders in September 2012.According to Marianne magazine, which broke the story, it was British tourists on 20 August who found the weapon lying in two metres of water.At first they thought it was a water pistol, but realised their mistake when they felt its weight.The discovery was made near the very camping site – Le Solitaire du Lac – where the al-Hillis were staying in their caravan, Marianne reported.Forensic experts are now examining the weapon, which has been badly damaged by its time under water, to see if it is indeed a P06 model.It is estimated that around 60,000 Luger P06s were manufactured. But the number of Luger pistols in general that were made is more like three million.Exhaustive investigations in France and the UK have left police no closer to understanding who carried out the al-Hilli murders and why.  Over the years a series of leads have been pursued then dropped.A British national of Iraqi birth, Saad al-Hilli was holidaying with his family in the picturesque countryside of Lake Annecy in eastern France.On the afternoon of 5 September, his body with those of his wife and mother-in-law were found in their car, its motor still running, on a forest road near the village of Chevaline. A passing cyclist had – like the other victims – been shot through the head.Poignantly, the two al-Hilli daughters, aged four and seven, survived. The older girl had been hit on the head with a pistol butt and was badly hurt. The younger, lying in the car under her mother's skirts, was not discovered till forensic experts began examining the scene many hours later.It was fragments from the pistol butt which enabled police to identify it as a Luger P06. The model is regarded more as a collector's item than a working weapon, which made the theory of a professional hit against the family seem less likely.Lake Annecy is only 50km from Switzerland, where the Luger P06 will have been familiar to older people from their military service. French police said many examples of the gun have been kept by families on either side of the border.Among the theories that have been entertained are that the murders were linked to a family row over money; that they were the work of a motiveless crank; and that the main target was the cyclist.Police were also briefly intrigued by the fact that al-Hilli's wife's first husband – an American – died of a heart attack just hours before the killings in France.

schema.headline: Alps murders: Luger in a lake gives hope for French cold case

title: South Korea: Police officer admits to closing missing person cases on Jeju to avoid work
description: A South Korean police officer has admitted to closing missing persons cases without investigating them in order to avoid additional work, according to
body: A South Korean police officer has admitted to closing missing persons cases without investigating them in order to avoid additional work, according to authorities.The officer, surnamed Bu, was arrested earlier this month after he was accused of prematurely closing cases on the popular holiday island Jeju and lying to missing persons' families.Amid mounting public criticism, police embarked on belated searches for several missing persons on the island, and have since discovered four bodies in recent weeks.The scandal has prompted President Lee Jae Myung to vow to reform the police, as the government prepares to give the police more powers.On Tuesday, the Jeju Provincial Police said Bu had falsely closed at least two high-profile cases and had been charged with forgery of public electronic records, obstruction of official duties and dereliction of duty.In both cases, Bu had falsely claimed he had contacted the missing persons and then prematurely closed their cases without confirming their whereabouts and safety.A police statement said that during their investigations into Bu, he had "stated to the effect that 'the missing person was a typical adult so I thought about it carelessly. If the case was not closed, there would have been a lot to take care of, and out of a sense of pressure over the case handover, I falsely closed it'."One of the cases involved a 37-year-old woman named Jang Mi-ran who went missing in May and was reported missing by her boyfriend. At the time, Bu had told Jang's boyfriend that he had spoken to her and she did not want to meet the police nor be contacted by her boyfriend. Authorities later said that this was a complete fabrication by Bu.Bu had entered this false information into the system, and also logged that Jang had died in a traffic accident, before closing the case, according to authorities.Jang's body was found near a palm tree plantation on Jeju last week.In another case where a man in his 60s was reported missing in July, Bu similarly falsely claimed that he had spoken to the man and that the man did not want to be contacted.The man was eventually found dead earlier this month.Police also said that they believe Bu could have prematurely closed another 25 missing persons cases, though in some of those cases the people were eventually confirmed to be alive and safe.Violent crime is rare in South Korea, where suicide rates are among the highest in the world.While more than 70,000 adults are reported missing in South Korea each year, 99% of them are marked as resolved within a month.This scandal comes at a politically sensitive time for the country's police.The government had recently passed laws to transfer full investigative power from the prosecutors to the police, a move they said was intended to curtail the prosecutors' influence in politics.However, this move has been unpopular among the public, who have for many years accused the police of corruption and incompetence.President Lee has vowed to reform the police in the wake of recent criticism.On Tuesday President Lee said that it was "regrettable" that because of a few "loach-like figures who muddy the well water", "the honour and pride of the majority of diligent police officers are being damaged".

schema.headline: South Korea: Police officer admits to closing missing person cases on Jeju to avoid work

title: Man arrested after Swiss rave shooting that killed 22-year-old woman
description: A 43-year-old Swiss man has been arrested following a shooting at a rave in Switzerland in which a woman was killed.Italian 22-year-old Maria Spinelli
body: A 43-year-old Swiss man has been arrested following a shooting at a rave in Switzerland in which a woman was killed.Italian 22-year-old Maria Spinelli was killed and several others injured at a techno rave being held at a horse racing track in Aarau, a town about 46km (29 miles) west of Zurich on Sunday.The shooting initiated a nearly 24-hour manhunt before Aarau cantonal police confirmed they apprehended the suspect shortly before 01:00 local time on Monday (23:00 GMT on Sunday)."The investigation into the exact sequence of events, the background and the possible motive is currently under way," police said in a statement. "At this time, it is assumed that the perpetrator acted alone."Police first received a report of shots fired at the Schachen race track at about 02:30 local time on Sunday.Spinelli died at the scene, while four men and a woman, aged between 24 and 27, were taken to hospital with injuries "ranging from minor to severe".An eyewitness told Swiss news outlet Blick that he had "suddenly heard the gunshots" minutes after the music stopped, initially believing they were fireworks.He said he was told to hide by a man and a woman, the latter of whom was shot.Organisers had expected 3,500 people to attend. Aarau, home to approximately 23,000 people, is less than 40km from the border with Germany, where local media reported police were supporting Swiss forces.The arrest marks a quick progression in the police investigation - on Sunday afternoon, the force in Aarau said it had no leads on the perpetrator and was unsure whether it was one person or several.Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni previously said she was confident Swiss authorities would "shed full light on what happened and find anyone responsible". Italy's foreign ministry said in a statement that it was sending officials to Zurich "to closely follow the investigation".Switzerland has one of the highest rates of gun ownership in Europe, although violent shootings are rare and tighter controls were introduced in recent years.The last major shooting occurred in 2001, when 14 members of the parliament and local government of Zug, near Lucerne, were killed by a gunman who then took his own life.

schema.headline: Man arrested after Swiss rave shooting that killed 22-year-old woman

title: Israel says senior Hamas member seized as strikes kill three during Gaza raid
description: Israel's defence minister says a senior member of the Palestinian armed group Hamas has been captured.Israel Katz was speaking after reports of a raid
body: Israel's defence minister says a senior member of the Palestinian armed group Hamas has been captured.Israel Katz was speaking after reports of a raid by Israeli special forces and an Israel-backed Palestinian militia in Gaza City.Israeli air strikes at the same time killed at least two children and a woman, local medics say.A third child was killed in a separate incident in central Gaza.The Israeli defence minister did not say who had captured the Hamas commander, whom he did not identify.But after meeting Israelis living in Netiv HaAsara, next to northern Gaza, Katz said the activity of Israeli forces in the territory "continues at all times"."A short time ago, a senior Hamas terrorist was arrested – and this is our policy: we do not wait for threats, but pursue Hamas terrorists, thwart them and destroy their terror infrastructures," he added.Earlier, Palestinians in a crowded part of western Gaza City had reported a heavy Israeli bombardment, with two vehicles hit and turned to wreckage.Videos captured chaotic scenes, with the sound of gunfire and the aftermath of strikes.Reports say that Israeli special forces and pro-Israeli Palestinian militiamen had entered the area, but their presence was discovered.  Some Israeli media suggest that only a local armed militia operated on the ground.A Palestinian security source told the BBC the target of the Israeli operation was a senior official in the Hamas internal security service.A spokesman for Gaza's Hamas-run government media office, Ismail al-Thawabta, said: "An Israeli special forces unit attempted to carry out a security operation in Gaza City, but the unit was exposed while carrying out the mission."The ensuing Israeli strikes "resulted in a number of people being killed and others injured, in addition to the deaths of several members of the special forces unit", he added.The Israeli military has only confirmed striking several targets in Gaza "in order to remove threats" to its troops, adding that none of them were injured.The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.Since then, more than 73,460 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

schema.headline: Israel says senior Hamas member seized as strikes kill three during Gaza raid

title: Russian attack hits rail workers in new deadly strikes on Kyiv
description: "Every day spent in war pushes humanity back, and every step taken towards peace fills humanity with new hope and enthusiasm," Modi said at a security
body: "Every day spent in war pushes humanity back, and every step taken towards peace fills humanity with new hope and enthusiasm," Modi said at a security summit in Kyrgyzstan.Modi, whose country's economy depends heavily on discounted oil from Moscow, has made several similar pleas to Putin since he launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Overnight in Kyiv, eight people were killed and fires were reported in three city districts. Another four people were killed in the nearby town of Boryspil where a residential building was hit.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Tuesday morning that nearly 350 rescue workers had been working through the night in Kyiv and the surrounding region after the latest strikes.In a post on social media, he said Russia had fired a "significant number of jet drones and ballistic missiles". The strikes mark the sixth day of sustained Russian drone and missile attacks on Kyiv, in what appears to be a strategy aimed at exhausting Ukrainian air defences and undermining civilian morale.Russia's military warned over the weekend that its forces were preparing to carry out "massive" strikes on Ukrainian energy facilities.Eight other Ukrainian regions were attacked, Zelensky said, adding that an Indian national was among the casualties.Ukraine's Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivsky later said the Indian man - who turned 26 on Tuesday - was killed in Boryspil. The overnight attacks come after 38 people were killed in Russian strikes on a weapons depot in the Kyiv region on Friday, causing shells, mines and drones to detonate.Separately, a drone attack hit a major Russian Baltic Sea port in Ust-Luga, triggering a fire, Leningrad regional Governor Aleksandr Drozdenko said.Ukraine says targets like Ust-Luga - which handles millions of tons of petroleum products each year - are legitimate as they help finance Moscow's war effort.

schema.headline: Russian attack hits rail workers in new deadly strikes on Kyiv

title: Northern Cyprus ferry: Couple's children missing after vessel capsizes
description: Ayten Bicer felt her 12-year-old daughter slip from her grasp and disappear as the ferry they were travelling on capsized off the coast of northern Cy
body: Ayten Bicer felt her 12-year-old daughter slip from her grasp and disappear as the ferry they were travelling on capsized off the coast of northern Cyprus on Sunday, killing eight people.Her daughter Miray and six-year-old son Memhet Asaf are among 20 people still missing after the vessel sunk while en route to Turkey from the coastal town of Kyrenia, in the self-proclaimed Turkish republic on Cyprus.She and her husband Hayri survived, and like many other families are waiting for news of their loved ones back in port as rescuers continue to search."She was saying, 'Don't let go'. And I didn't let go of my daughter. I swear, I didn't let her go," Bicer told reporters through tears.Bicer said a suitcase fell on top of her, which forced her daughter from her grip. She managed to grab hold of her daughter's foot, but her shoes were coated in engine oil from the overturned vessel and she slipped through her hands."It was slippery everywhere. It was like oil. She slipped out of my hand," she recalled.The family was returning to Turkey after a holiday on the Mediterranean island."We couldn't intervene, we lost our children," Hayri Bicer said. "Two of my three children are gone. We left them. We are leaving them on this island as we go."The vessel had been carrying 259 passengers and eight crew members. Nineteen passengers are currently being treated in hospitals in northern Cyprus, local authorities say.The eight crew members, including the ship's captain, and one other man were formally arrested on Monday. They will be detained for three days, while warrants have been issued for several other people. The privately owned ferry left the popular holiday resort of Kyrenia at about 12:30 (09:30 GMT), en route to the town of Tasucu in Turkey.It had been scheduled to travel to Turkey on Saturday but its journey was delayed due to severe storms hitting the island. The seas were still rough on Sunday.Some eyewitness accounts say the double-hulled ferry jolted violently before slamming onto the sea surface, with part of its bow bursting open on impact.Ünal Üstel, prime minister of the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC), which is only recognised by Turkey, told local media the boat was hit by two waves before it capsized. While the captain of the vessel was trying to recover from the first wave, a second wave hit and it began taking on water, he said.The boat has completely sunk and is lying at a depth of 514m (1,686ft), officials say.Debris remains scattered across the water, including a black wheelie suitcase bobbing on the surface and a sheet of steel that appeared to have broken away from the ferry.Authorities are attempting to recover the vessel's black box recorder to establish what happened.A ship will be arriving from Turkey on Tuesday to help with search efforts, TRNC President Tufan Erhurman said. Meanwhile, a three-day period of national mourning began on Monday.The ferry - a high-speed 40m long, 10m wide Filo Jet vessel - sails under the flag of Turkey, according to Marine Traffic.Filo Denizcilik, the company which operates the capsized passenger boat, said it was "deeply saddened by the tragic accident".The TRNC controls the northern third of the island of Cyprus, which has been divided since 1974.

schema.headline: Northern Cyprus ferry: Couple's children missing after vessel capsizes

title: Germany says Russia behind Leipzig airport drone attack
description: Germany has said Russia was responsible for last month's drone attack at Leipzig's airport. A drone carrying an explosive device was discovered at Lei
body: Germany has said Russia was responsible for last month's drone attack at Leipzig's airport. A drone carrying an explosive device was discovered at Leipzig/Halle Airport in eastern Germany, close to Ukrainian cargo planes, on 4 August.It failed to explode as the detonator was apparently faulty, and investigators suspect a second drone collided with a cargo aircraft nearby. A third drone was reportedly found near the airport 10 days later.Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said the Leipzig airport attack followed the "well-established pattern of Russian hybrid operations in Europe" and the assumption was that Germany would be targeted again.He said the that examination of the equipment used along with intelligence findings proved Russian involvement in the attack.German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, who was standing beside Dobrindt at a press conference in Berlin, said he would order the closure of the Russian consulate in Bonn, and the contract for the Russian House in Berlin will also be terminated - which many observers have said has been used for espionage and to spread Russian propaganda.He also announced tighter entry controls for Russian nationals and vowed to increase pressure on Moscow's shadow fleet - old tankers used by Russia to circumvent Western sanctions following its invasion of Ukraine in 2022.Wadephul said he had summoned the Russia's ambassador to Germany, Sergei Nechayev. He was seen arriving at the foreign ministry shortly after the announcement.Maria Zakharova, spokesperson for Russia's foreign ministry, said Moscow would respond in a "mirror-image" fashion to Germany's measures."Berlin is sponsoring terrorism", she told the German Press Agency in reference to its military and economic support provided to Ukraine.There have been previous suggestions that the Goethe-Institut in Moscow would have to cease operations if the Germans went through with closing Russian House.Security experts had speculated that Russia may have been responsible, however Russia has always rejected claims of involvement. Leipzig/Halle Airport in eastern Germany is used by the Germany military and Nato allies for the transport of military goods and also serves as a base for Ukraine's Antonov Airlines - which carries most of the country's aerial cargo.The head of Nato, Mark Rutte, said the organisation "stands in full solidarity with Germany"."The evidence is clear. And I welcome the measures announced by Germany in response," he wrote on X.The issue was due to be discussed at a meeting of EU foreign ministers in Ireland later on Tuesday.EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on X: "We are united in our resolve to stand against Russian aggression. We will deter anyone who seeks to undermine our freedom and security."She added that the EU was preparing additional sanctions against Russia.Meanwhile, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "Russian attempts to undermine our united resolve and our willingness to support Ukraine are futile and doomed to fail."Germany is one of several Nato member states to have reported drone sightings at airports, military and industrial sites over the last year.Berlin has until now been tight-lipped about who may have been behind the Leipzig attack, except to say the "foreign powers" may have been involved. US media had already reported that American officials had linked the incident to Russia.Berlin has warned that the country is the "daily target" of hybrid warfare, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz warned last week that those who carried out hostile acts against Germany would "pay a price".The government is looking to boost the powers of its intelligence services, which have long been criticised as relatively toothless, to counter such threats.Germany is a key backer of Ukraine with Merz forthright in his support for Kyiv.It is not hard to imagine why Ukrainian cargo planes at a key German logistics hub might be in Moscow's sights.But this announcement comes at a delicate moment for Merz's government.A key state election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt could propel the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) into power at a state-level for the very first time.The AfD, which is Germany's biggest opposition party, wants to stop sending support to Ukraine and re-open ties with Russia.In a separate development, German police say they are investigating the discovery of improvised explosive and incendiary devices at a power substation in the eastern state of Brandenburg on Tuesday.A power line was damaged, which caused a temporary outage. It is not known who planted the devices.

schema.headline: Germany says Russia behind Leipzig airport drone attack

title: Uniqlo, Muji: Japan Inc is betting big on India as China risks deepen
description: India's commerce minister Piyush Goyal led the country's largest-ever business delegation to Japan last week in a bid to expand trade and investment t
body: India's commerce minister Piyush Goyal led the country's largest-ever business delegation to Japan last week in a bid to expand trade and investment ties between the two countries. His visit came as Japan's deepening push into Asia's third largest economy has become increasingly more apparent. If you visit a shopping mall or a high street in Mumbai, Delhi or Bengaluru, it's hard to miss the growing number of Japanese consumer brands that have set up shop across India. Apparel giants Uniqlo and Muji and premium sneakers company Onitsuka Tiger have been around for a while, but are rapidly expanding.Niche players are also here - Nitori, a Japanese furniture maker, entered the market recently, while convenience store chain Lawson, external is on its way, with a plan to reportedly open 10,000 stores by 2050 in India, starting with Mumbai.It's not just retail. At a time when foreign lenders have been exiting their Indian bank portfolios, Japanese banks are aggressively bidding for Indian financial assets.MUFG Bank - Japan's largest bank - closed a deal to buy 20% of Indian shadow lender Shriram Finance for $4.4bn last year in what was the biggest ever foreign investment in India's financial sector.Last year also saw Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation (SMBC) becoming the largest shareholder in India's Yes Bank with a 24.22% stake.Japan Inc is now the largest contributor to India's booming ecosystem of global capability centres (GCCs) in the Asia Pacific.More than 100 Japanese firms operate these GCCs in the country, according to a recent Deloitte report, external. GCCs are offshore innovation hubs of multinationals that perform business critical functions such as R&D, corporate strategy and artificial intelligence development among a plethora of other key jobs."Japanese companies are having to look to India for growth. With the local population declining for the past 16-17 years there isn't just a slowdown in domestic demand, but a permanent shrinking of the market," Vipul Nath Jindal, Founder of Next Bharat Ventures, an impact fund backed by Suzuki Motor Corporation, which recently announced a $200m fund in India, told the BBC.At the same time, Japan's traditional markets for expansion have become increasingly less attractive, he says."Investment into China has fallen sharply amid geopolitical tensions and changing economic dynamics, the US market is more challenging because of tariffs and domestic competition, and the market size of other Southeast Asian economies is limited."Against this backdrop, India has become a natural target market for Japanese companies to drive long-term business growth.Economic ties between the countries gathered pace at a government-to-government level when they signed an agreement to liberalise trade nearly a decade-and-a-half ago.After Prime Minister Narendra Modi came to power in 2014, he elevated the relationship to a "special strategic and global partnership", setting a target of doubling the number of Japanese companies in India and launching marquee projects like India's first bullet train between Mumbai and Ahmedabad, built using Japanese Shinkansen technology.But now, it is Japanese private firms that are driving business expansion in this latest investment up-cycle.At a landmark summit in July held during Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's first official visit to Delhi, Japanese companies announced $12.5bn in investments. They signed around 120 agreements in sectors ranging from semiconductors to green energy. In fact, Goyal has said Japan could prematurely meet its target of investing 10 trillion yen in the country. Beyond the large corporations, several Japanese small and medium-sized companies (SMEs) are also actively looking at tapping the Indian market, says Jindal.Hamamatsu City - where companies like Suzuki, Honda and Yamaha were founded and which has one of the highest concentrations of manufacturing SMEs in Japan - recently set up the Hamamatsu India Committee to explore how the city's small companies could expand into India.The rising interest in India has accompanied a fall in net Japanese investment in China which, as Toshiro Nishizaewa of the University of Tokyo wrote recently, external, is a reflection of "Japanese firms' autonomous market diversification strategies - a commercially driven reallocation of capital rather than a policymaker-led geopolitical shift from China to India".But Japanese firms aren't abandoning China en masse. What they are doing is "reducing concentration risk after several years of supply chain disruptions and geopolitical tensions", Shruti Pandalai, India Chair at the Sydney-based Lowy Institute think tank, told the BBC.India acts as a hedge against China-related risks, but there is also a growing overlap between Tokyo's economic security priorities and Delhi's manufacturing ambitions, which has strengthened the relationship despite significant political turnover in Tokyo, she says."With each successive government the targets have risen rather than fallen. That suggests the relationship has moved beyond leader-level diplomacy and become embedded in bureaucratic, corporate and strategic planning on both sides."For Delhi, which is starved of foreign investment, the Japanese money comes at a crucial time. India's burgeoning trade deficit with China has been a matter of grave concern and closer Japan-India cooperation could gradually reduce China's leverage in areas such as critical minerals and advanced manufacturing over the longer term, according to Pandalai.But challenges to expanding the full scope of this relationship are many, say experts."Japan remains deeply integrated into Chinese manufacturing networks, while India's engagement is more uneven but still significant in key sectors," writes Pratnashree Basu from the Observer Research Foundation for the online portal Scroll, external. "Economic interdependence, in this sense, constrains the scope for coordinated measures as these would impose significant commercial costs or provoke direct economic retaliation from China."Also, India remains a tough country to do business. Tax uncertainties, bureaucratic red tape, delays in land and environmental approvals are all long-documented challenges for foreign investors, including the Japanese.An ex-Japanese minister recently publicly blamed the government in Delhi for delays in the bullet train project, saying India kept "pushing its own self interest" and "flipping on promises" - criticism which the Indian government immediately rebuffed, external.Chinese state media, external was quick to pick up on the "rifts", using the incident as an example to highlight the gaps in India's ability to enforce contracts. It underscores why, even as it seals a raft of big-ticket economic and defence agreements, Delhi will need to work doubly hard to ensure Japanese investment momentum isn't disrupted - especially given its growing struggle to attract sustained foreign capital from elsewhere.Follow BBC News India on Instagram, external, YouTube,, external X, external and Facebook, external.

schema.headline: Uniqlo, Muji: Japan Inc is betting big on India as China risks deepen

title: The jury's options in Lindsay Clancy's murder trial
description: Not just guilty or not - The jury's options in Lindsay Clancy's murder trialImage source, ReutersByAna Faguyreporting from court in MassachusettsUpdat
body: Not just guilty or not - The jury's options in Lindsay Clancy's murder trialImage source, ReutersByAna Faguyreporting from court in MassachusettsUpdated 8 hours agoLindsay Clancy's murder trial has gripped the American public for the last five weeks.The 36-year-old former nurse killed her three small children in the basement of their family home in Massachusetts.Charged with three counts of first-degree murder, she does not dispute killing her two sons and daughter in 2023.But her lawyer argues she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time, and therefore could not distinguish right from wrong.The prosecution, on the other hand, argues Clancy made a calculated, intentional decision to kill them and knew right from wrong in that moment.On Tuesday morning, after three days of deliberation, a jury of nine women and three men will continue to deliberate, with several options before them:not guilty not guilty by reason of insanityfirst-degree murdersecond-degree murdermanslaughterNot guilty / not guilty by reason of insanityThis hinges on the postpartum psychosis defence - her legal team argued that Clancy hallucinated a voice that told her to kill the children.Expert witnesses told the court how severe this illness can be, and family members testified about Clancy's state of mind.Under Massachusetts law, there is no burden on Clancy to prove her mental illness and that she lacked criminal responsibility.Rather, it is on the prosecution to prove beyond reasonable doubt that she was criminally responsible when she killed her children, criminal defence lawyer Elyse Hershon told the BBC.They can do this by either proving beyond reasonable doubt that she didn't suffer from a mental illness at the time or that, while she had a mental illness, she still controlled her actions and knew they were wrong.A not guilty verdict would mean Clancy went free but that is considered highly unlikely. Much more likely is a not guilty by reason of insanity, which would result in Clancy being detained at a hospital."The case really comes down to where she is going to serve the rest of her life; the defence thinks it should be a psychiatric facility, the prosecution thinks it should be in a state prison," Hershon said.Figure caption, Watch: What is postpartum psychosis and why is it central in the Lindsay Clancy trial?First-degree murderThis is the most serious potential outcome for Clancy - being found guilty of first-degree murder, which is the intentional and premeditated killing of another person.In the state of Massachusetts, this conviction carries a mandatory sentence of life in prison without the possibility of parole.As Heather Cucolo, a New York Law School professor and expert in mental health law, put it to the BBC, Clancy would effectively need to be seen as "a monster in the jury's eyes" if they pick this outcome.Jurors would have to find there was extreme atrocity or cruelty or premeditation or both to convict Clancy of this, and it would mean the prosecution had proven there were no mitigating factors.In this case, mental disease or defect - as the law describes it - could be a mitigating factor.Prosecutor Jennifer Sprague said during closing arguments there was no dispute Clancy was suffering from mental illness but it was not so severe that she didn't know right from wrong.Expert witnesses for the prosecution cast doubt on whether Clancy actually heard the voice that she said ordered her to kill her children.Second-degree murderThis is a catch-all for any murder that is not first-degree, under Massachusetts law.It applies to unlawful killings committed with malice or extreme recklessness, but without prior planning."For this verdict, the jurors may not be convinced that the actions leading up to the murder rose to the level of pre-planned [or] premeditated but that instead, Clancy consciously saw an opportunity to commit the killings at the specified time," Cucolo said.In the case of second-degree murder, Clancy would also face a life sentence - but with the possibility of parole.ManslaughterThe jury received yet another option when the judge allowed them to find Clancy guilty of manslaughter - previously a point of contention between the defence and the prosecution.A manslaughter conviction would mean Clancy unintentionally killed "by wanton and reckless conduct", which carries a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison per count.The manslaughter option says that through an involuntary intoxication, in this case an overprescription of her medication, Clancy experienced a mental defect that was a mitigator in her understanding what she was doing, Hershon said.Intent is an important distinction between a verdict like manslaughter and the two murder verdicts, experts said."This option allows the jury to accept that the murders were not planned or calculated but that instead Clancy made a split-second decision to act," Cucolo said.The prosecution is not obligated to demonstrate that she intended to cause the children's deaths for there to be a manslaughter conviction, she added.

schema.headline: The jury's options in Lindsay Clancy's murder trial

title: Duane "Keffe D" Davis found guilty of 1996 murder of rapper Tupac Shakur
description: Former gang boss Duane "Keffe D" Davis has been found guilty of orchestrating the murder of Tupac Shakur - the first conviction in a cold case that ha
body: Former gang boss Duane "Keffe D" Davis has been found guilty of orchestrating the murder of Tupac Shakur - the first conviction in a cold case that has intrigued hip-hop fans for nearly 30 years.The jury found him guilty of one count of murder with a deadly weapon for the rap superstar's death in a drive-by shooting in Las Vegas on 7 September 1996.Dressed in a black suit, the 63-year-old stood impassively in the Las Vegas court as the verdict was read, before saying he would appeal. During the trial, the court heard a recording of a police interview in 2008 in which Davis said he was in the car from which shots were fired, but did not himself fire the bullets that killed Shakur.Prosecutors argued that although Davis, a former leader of the South Side Compton Crips street gang, did not himself fire the gun, he ordered the shooting and supplied the gun that his nephew Orlando Anderson used to open fire.Anderson died in an unrelated shooting in 1998, having denied involvement in the killing of Shakur.As the verdict was read out on Monday, Shakur's relatives held hands, some hugging and crying.Shakur was 25 when he was slain at the height of his career as one of rap's most influential voices. He has sold more than 75 million records worldwide.For 30 years, the case remained one of America's most famous cold cases, spurring countless conspiracies - but never a conviction, until now. Throughout the trial, Davis' defence team tried to persuade jurors that his comments were fiction - bravado and exaggeration intended to sell books and make money. In closing arguments, his lawyer Michael Sanft urged the jury to discredit his client as a liar who just told tales to sell books. "There's no proof," he told the jury. But within hours of the jury being handed the case on Monday, they reached a guilty verdict. Just before the court emptied out, Clark County District Court Judge Carli Kierny set Davis' sentencing for 13 October.While reading out some procedural steps in the case, Davis appeared to interrupt by raising his hand."I would like my stuff," he told the judge, mentioning some personal items including his phone.He continued: "I would like to appeal this matter." The judge explained that this could happen after sentencing.Clark County District Attorney Steven Wolfson said on Tuesday that Davis is facing a minimum of 40 years in prison, and that prosecutors won't seek to add gang enhancements to his sentence in large part due to his age."I don't know a defendant convicted of murder who doesn't plan to appeal," Wolfson said at a news conference a day after the verdict. "We feel confident in the strength of our case."

title: The US-Canada trade war in 5 charts
description: The US and Canada appear no closer to resolving their ongoing trade dispute. Tensions have been simmering between the two neighbours since President D
body: The US and Canada appear no closer to resolving their ongoing trade dispute. Tensions have been simmering between the two neighbours since President Donald Trump returned to the White House just over 18 months ago, and unleashed a wide-ranging global programme of tariffs.Canada was one of the first countries the Trump administration hit with levies, and is one of two countries to respond with its own reciprocal measures.Currently, the US has hit Canada's key sectors of steel, aluminium, lumber and automobiles with tariffs, and last week imposed an additional 50% levy on about C$28bn ($20bn; £15bn) of Canadian goods.Canada has hit back with its own counter-tariffs on American goods, announcing on Tuesday what it calls a "dollar-for-dollar" and "strategic" retaliation designed to match the US tariffs.With no resolution in sight, how has this enduring trade war affected Canada and the US, and what could come next?Here are five charts to help break it all down. The US economy is much larger and the impact of Canada's counter-tariffs won't be as stark.But some states will feel the pain of Canada's retaliation more than others, with tariffs levied on C$28bn worth of US goods from steel to furniture, cosmetics and toilet paper, as of 8 September.According to data by Statistics Canada, the swing state of Ohio will be hardest hit, with C$3.2bn - or 12% - of its exports soon to be tariffed by Canada, followed by Illinois and Pennsylvania.For Ohio, it's the tax on steel that will particularly hurt, as well as the tax on laundry machines. In Illinois, where farm equipment giant John Deere is based, it will be the new tariffs on farm and construction equipment. Derek Holt, an economist with Scotiabank, noted that Canada's counter-tariffs appear to be "very deliberately oriented" towards some swing states that could decide the US balance of power in the upcoming midterm elections.Some businesses are adapting to find customers elsewhere. Matteo Sgaramella, who owns Toronto-based menswear clothing company Outclass, told the BBC he has started attending trunk shows in Paris instead of New York, helping him reach more customers in Europe."The reception has been amazing," he said, adding that some European stores are particularly enthused about supporting Canadian products due to the ongoing trade war with the US."We're kind of seen as the one country that's kind of standing up to the Americans right now," Sgaramella said.Other businesses, however, are struggling to diversify their trade, particularly in Ontario manufacturing sectors that are deeply integrated with the US.A recent report by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce pointed out three such regions in Ontario - Oshawa, London and Kitchener-Cambridge-Waterloo - as being particularly vulnerable."These cities remain heavily tied to the US market, while growth in exports outside the US has been limited or insufficient to offset broader weakness in trade activity and local economic conditions," the report said.While some businesses are lagging, foreign direct investment into Canada hit C$96.8 billion in 2025, the highest inflow of capital to the Canadian economy since 2007.Canada's economy also strongly rebounded in the second quarter of 2026 to 3.3% growth in the country's GDP, thanks to a jump in exports and domestic investment. These latest figures have warded off recession concerns, at least for now.Carney is hoping to attract even more investment. In September, his government will host the first-ever Canada Investment Summit, bringing major investors, CEOs and business leaders to Toronto for two days.

schema.headline: The US-Canada trade war in 5 charts

title: Nepal floods: The remote Nepal-China border crossing at the heart of a Himalayan tragedy
description: The video lasts only seconds.A dark wall appears from behind the buildings at Gyirong, on the Chinese side of the Nepal-Tibet border. At first, it loo
body: The video lasts only seconds.A dark wall appears from behind the buildings at Gyirong, on the Chinese side of the Nepal-Tibet border. At first, it looks almost like a black cloud. Then it gathers shape and speed: water, mud, boulders, ice and rock surging down the valley. The CCTV footage, whose timestamp reads 10:59:53, went viral.For many, it was the first visual evidence of the sheer scale of the destruction that was unfolding.What happened in the minutes that followed is still difficult to reconstruct. But fragments of video and satellite imagery show much of the border complex swept away, with buildings that once crowded the valley floor simply gone.Electronic immigration records from Nepal's Rasuwagadhi border post are filling some gaps, as well as insights from its only surviving staff member. Tika Ram Pokharel, who happened to be in Kathmandu sitting an exam on the day, tells the BBC the crossing was unusually busy when floodwater hit."This is a historic travel route between Kathmandu and Tibet," explains Kathmandu-based hydrologist Ajay Dixit. "The area is geologically vulnerable, characterised by deep gorges and steep rivers that flow at high velocity, carry heavy sediment and can bring down huge boulders."It is a place where pilgrims heading towards Mount Kailash cross paths with traders travelling between Nepal and China, truck drivers, customs officials, tourists and people who live along the border.On the morning of the flood, more than 100 Indians may have been in or around the crossing. At least 275 Indians remain missing in Nepal, according to India's foreign ministry.Nepal's immigration department has been trying to reconstruct who passed through Rasuwagadhi in the final hours before the disaster.Electronic records show that 89 Nepali and foreign nationals had cleared immigration to leave Nepal for Tibet, while four people had registered their entry into Nepal.The immigration system recorded its final transaction at 08:35:03 local time (10:52 Tibet time), less than 10 minutes before the torrent appeared on the CCTV footage at Gyirong.Four immigration employees, including the head of the Rasuwagadhi office, went missing in the floods. His body was later recovered far downstream. The female official who recorded the final transactions is still missing.Among the foreign nationals recorded leaving Nepal that morning were 32 Indians, 12 Chinese nationals and nine Americans, as well as citizens of Britain, Canada, Australia and Italy.Tika Ram Pokharel, the surviving senior immigration assistant at Rasuwagadhi, says the electronic records capture only part of what was happening at the border that morning.The immigration office stood at Ghatte Khola Bazar, about 1.5km north of Timure, a small trading settlement clustered around the crossing. From there, it was another 2km to the Friendship Bridge marking the border with Tibet. Along that stretch were shops, hotels and parking areas where travellers and vehicles gathered before crossing.The Nepalese immigration office opened at 08:00, Pokharel says. Once travellers had cleared immigration, they could continue towards the border or wait in the area before crossing.When Pokharel called a colleague at 08:20 that morning, he was told the crossing was unusually busy. Around 300 to 400 people were waiting to leave Nepal for Tibet, he says, while others arriving from the Chinese side were also in the area."Those who completed the immigration formalities that morning, I don't think were able to complete their immigration process on the Chinese side," Pokharel tells the BBC.Pokharel says it took 15 to 20 minutes to walk from the Nepalese immigration office to the bridge after travellers had cleared immigration. Travellers arriving late the previous afternoon sometimes had to wait until the border reopened the next morning, while those travelling in groups or by bus would often wait for everyone to clear immigration before moving on together.That makes it difficult to know where those 89 people were when the flood struck.At 08:37 - less than two minutes after the immigration system recorded its final transaction - seismic instruments detected movement in the mountains above the border, according to a timeline compiled by Nepal's Centre of Hydrology and Water Resources Research. Researchers later attributed the signal to the collapse of part of a glacier that triggered the flood.China said the mudslide reached the border crossing from its origin in around seven minutes.People at the crossing could have been making their way towards the bridge, waiting in Ghatte Khola or preparing to cross towards the Chinese facility. Exactly where each person was remains unclear.And Ghatte Khola itself was far more than a waiting area. Pokharel says 50 to 60 houses stood there, alongside hotels, local businesses and four hydropower offices.It was also the final stop for buses from Kathmandu, and a base for drivers, helpers, tourist guides and cargo workers waiting for customs clearance. Travellers heading into Tibet often queued there from the previous day."My 40-50 close friends are missing," Pokharel said. Pokharel believes the toll there could be far higher than official figures suggest, estimating that "2,000 to 2,500 people" may have been caught in the flood. The figure is his estimate and has not been independently verified.The immigration office itself stood about 100 metres above the river, Pokharel says. But during the flood, the water appeared to surge even higher. He initially hoped his missing colleagues might have escaped to grazing land several kilometres away.For some of the Indian pilgrims at the border, the morning had begun almost casually. They made video calls and reels for relatives back home, showing them the mountains as they waited for the Chinese immigration office to open.Sudipto Bhattacharya was receiving messages from his wife, Subhrasree Chakraborty, who was travelling with a group of more than 60 people. At 07:57 Nepal time, she sent him a photograph of the departure stamp in her passport: Nepalese immigration was done. Six minutes later, at 08:03, she sent another message: "We are waiting to enter China." Then the messages stopped.Among those at the Chinese immigration facility was a group of 77 pilgrims associated with the Isha Foundation, returning from Mount Kailash. They, along with three staff members, were unaccounted for after the flood swept through the area.When a 21-member Chinese rescue team reached Gyirong on 28 August, one rescuer told Chinese state media: "As far as the eye could see, there was nothing but ruins."The crossing had only recently recovered from another major flood. In July 2025, flooding shut Rasuwagadhi for nearly six months. It reopened on 1 January after China built a temporary bridge.Traffic had since returned. Chinese border authorities say more than 100,000 people had passed through Gyirong by June, while Nepali immigration records show 53,742 arrivals and departures at Rasuwagadhi in the year to mid-July. The two figures are based on different reporting periods and counting systems, making a direct comparison difficult.Indians were the largest group recorded at the Nepali immigration point, followed by Nepalis and Chinese.Gyirong had also become one of the main arteries linking Nepal and China.Posh Raj Pandey, chairman emeritus of the Kathmandu-based South Asia Watch on Trade, Economics and Environment, says Rasuwagadhi is one of Nepal's two main trading points with China, alongside Tatopani, and accounts for about a third of Nepal's $2.95bn trade with its northern neighbour.Around 60 to 70 trucks passed through the gorge each day, carrying electronics, machinery, vehicles, fruit, clothing and other goods towards Kathmandu. Pandey says the route also handled about 80% of Nepal's electric-vehicle imports from China.Its closure has left Nepal increasingly dependent on Tatopani - which Chinese authorities have also temporarily closed, external because of landslide risks on the Nepali side, the Kathmandu Post reports. The crossing also lies along the proposed route of the railway connecting the region to Kathmandu, part of plans by Nepal and China to develop a trans-Himalayan rail network."Nepal should develop an alternative China trade route and reconsider its wider development strategy, including its heavy concentration of hydropower projects along the same river system," Pandey says. "We have put all eggs here. We need to develop an alternative border port."Across the border, Pokharel was left thinking about conversations he had with the colleagues who were now missing.The previous year's flood had made staff at the Rasuwagadhi immigration office acutely aware of the danger. At night, he says, they sometimes "felt vibrations" and went outside to check the river. They had even discussed among themselves about escaping uphill if another flood struck."But my friends could not get that chance," he said.

schema.headline: Nepal floods: The remote Nepal-China border crossing at the heart of a Himalayan tragedy

title: 'I've never been to Afghanistan': Six million deportees forced to start over under the Taliban
description: Figure caption, Watch: BBC's Lyse Doucet reports on the biggest cross-border movement of peopleByLyse DoucetChief international correspondentReporting
body: Figure caption, Watch: BBC's Lyse Doucet reports on the biggest cross-border movement of peopleByLyse DoucetChief international correspondentReporting fromTorkham crossing and KabulThe elderly grimace, hobbling on crutches, and wide-eyed children stare, cradling chickens carried from homes they were forced to leave behind."It feels good to be in my own country," 35-year-old Nazia says, just minutes after she crosses from Pakistan, where she was born, into Afghanistan.The Torkham crossing, known as "Zero Point", is where one hard life ends and another begins."But I've never been to Afghanistan before and many people here don't even have enough bread to eat," Nazia sighs as she heads, two of her children in tow, toward registration counters festooned with white and black Taliban flags.Nearly her entire family, eight sisters and their offspring, were deported to Afghanistan this year from Pakistan or Iran.They are part of the biggest cross-border movement of people anywhere in the world.Millions of Afghans have fled across the borders to Pakistan and Iran for decades – seeking refuge or employment - and the number escaping Afghanistan has continued to rise since the Taliban takeover in August 2021.Most are now being forced to return as these two neighbours crack down on undocumented migrants. Nazia and her family were undocumented but the UN and human rights groups say the security sweep is reaching far beyond that group to include registered Afghans too. Even Pakistan now publicly says that Afghans with Proof of Registration cards are not exempt.The expulsions show no sign of stopping. Image source, AFPImage caption, Trucks carrying returnees parked along the highway near the border The number forced to return this year from Pakistan and Iran has already reached another million, according to the UN's Refugee Agency, the UNHCR."In a little under three years, we've seen six million people, a population that is itself the size of a small country, come back to Afghanistan," observes Charlie Goodlake, spokesperson for the UNHCR in Afghanistan."We've never seen in recent history a return movement on this scale," he underlines, standing in the baking heat in the tented village close to the border.It's a desolate landscape of tarpaulin and plastic shelters, many now tattered and torn, erected by the UN and other aid agencies to provide refuge for a few nights for a people arriving with nowhere to go.Many returnees have not set foot in Afghanistan for decades; many like Nazia have never been here at all."I left 45 years ago during the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and most of my brothers were born in Pakistan," explains Sarwar, who arrived a few days earlier with seven brothers and their families in a convoy of 40 people and the jumble of their worldly goods packed into a lumbering Pakistani lorry."We spent a long time there, so of course I felt heartbroken when they forced us out of our home," he says. "But, despite all that pain, I am also happy because I am finally free of harassment by Pakistan's police."Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Afghan returnees deported from Pakistan arriving at the Torkham crossing Every family we met told us they had experienced prejudice and harassment by authorities in Pakistan.The Pakistan government has not responded to the BBC's questions, but a foreign ministry spokesman told a briefing in Islamabad on Sunday that "the Government of Pakistan undertakes the necessary measures to prevent any instance of harassment or maltreatment of Afghan nationals in Pakistan. If such incidents have taken place, they are sporadic and are dealt with fully in accordance with the law". Both Pakistan and Iran say it's past time for Afghans to go home, accusing some of posing a security risk, and others of being a financial burden.The expulsions from Pakistan and alleged abuse intensified after a major escalation in fighting between Pakistan and Afghanistan last October. In February, Human Rights Watch highlighted "door-to-door raids, late-night home searches and arrests without warrants".In Iran, which claimed last year to host more than four million undocumented Afghans, the mass deportations were accelerated after its 12-day war with Israel and the US in June 2025.The New York based Centre for Human Rights in Iran accused the authorities of using the post-war climate to "cast suspicion on Afghan migrants - accusing them of espionage and branding them as potential spies for Israel".The UN's refugee agency continues to underscore the humanitarian principle that any return should be "voluntary, safe and dignified".But in Torkham, Sarwar's sister-in-law Zarina laments the precarious future they face: "We have no resources to start a business or earn a living, and we don't even own a tent to live in".Image caption, Zarina, 40, is among the million Afghan who have returned this year alone Inside the barren transit tent, which provides little escape from scorching 41C heat, Zarina sits alongside an anxious huddle of women and their children. Are they worried about the future for women and girls in a country where the Taliban has barred women from much of public life, including secondary school and university?Forty-year-old Zarina turns to make a sweeping gesture with her arm: "Look at them, they're all girls. Of course I'm worried."Some returnees are not just worried; they're terrified."I don't leave this house," a former Afghan security guard, first deported from Iran and then Pakistan, nervously tells us when we meet him far from the border in what he hopes is a safe house. "We are all living in fear including my wife and children who are also afraid to go outside."He dismisses the Taliban government's amnesty, announced days after their return to power which declared that former government officials, security personnel and civil servants would not face retaliation and were encouraged to return to work."I have no trust in their amnesty because many of my colleagues have been killed." He says his case had been registered with the UN but was deported before he could be transferred to a safer country. Financial hardship magnifies the pain. The steep cuts in foreign aid worldwide are especially sharp in Afghanistan where the Taliban are still stuck in sanctions linked to terrorism and human rights.Pakistan confirmed on Sunday that 16,000 vulnerable Afghans have now been granted, on humanitarian grounds, a temporary exemption from being deported – a decision welcomed by the UN.  But sources estimate that the number of Afghans in Pakistan at risk of serious harm, including women and girls who would be denied education, could be as high as 250,000.Image caption, Zarina says she is worried about the future of the girls who cannot attend secondary school and university in Taliban-run AfghanistanAt the graceful foreign ministry compound in Kabul, Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi tries to put on a brave face."There's no doubt that we need some help," he admits. "There is pressure due to their return but in the long run, it will benefit them as well as Afghanistan."In the first years after the Taliban swept to power in 2021, some of their ministers made light of humanitarian issues, saying God would provide. The UN now estimates that 21.9 million people, nearly half the country, need assistance this year to survive. The UN's children agency, UNICEF, said last week that one million children faced "life-threatening" malnutrition."No country in the world could handle this kind of crisis on its own," UNHCR spokesperson Goodlake assesses, while acknowledging Taliban government efforts to help returnees as they arrive.But, he adds, "We also know that many of the restrictions and edicts they put in place, particularly on women and girls, don't help us elicit international support".Muttaqi reiterates his government's line that matters like girl's education are "internal issues" for Afghans to resolve.The severe restrictions on the lives of girls and women is one of the major issues in the Taliban's international relationships and that has cost them. Five years on, only one country, Russia, has formally recognised their rule.But when asked about this, Muttaqi points to the deepening diplomatic and economic ties with neighbours such as China and India, as well as Central Asian states. As for Kabul's relative isolation from western nations, he asks, "those who didn't have relationships with us over the past five years, what have they achieved?"He answers his own question: "Nothing."We heard that word - "nothing" - from every family we met at Zero Point, but in a much different sense. All were embarking on the hardest of homecomings, beginning all over again - with almost nothing.

schema.headline: 'I've never been to Afghanistan': Six million deportees forced to start over under the Taliban
